meta.title: 40 albums · 40 days
about: Music has been the through-line of my whole life. I've been to countless shows, I've played various instruments, and I've spent years collecting records. Turning 40 felt like the right time to look back at some of the albums that got me here.

These aren't my 40 favorite albums. I couldn't pick those if my life depended on it. Plenty of these would make that list, and every one would be in my top 100, but this list is about more than favorites.

Every one of these is tied to a place and a time. I can still remember the first time I heard each of them, or what I was doing when I played them the most. On a crappy Panasonic RX-DS515 boombox on the floor of my bedroom. Driving around in my car at 16, 17, 18 with the windows down. Sleeping on the floor of the bus on the way to a different college town for a lacrosse game. Screen-printing gig posters in the art building at Mizzou. Moving to Chicago, then Denver, then Chicago again, then Denver again.

These albums are special to me in other ways. Some of them introduced me to a genre I didn't know I'd love, or pulled me back into one I'd walked away from years earlier. Some had me digging through the band's back catalog until they became one of my favorite bands. And some just weirdly fit my life at that stage.
Each day you'll find where I was when I first heard it, and why it stuck.

albums.title: Weezer (Green Album)
albums.discovered: Late spring 2001, from a friend's "cool" older brother
blurb: School was out. It was the summer before my freshman year of high school, and I spent every day of it blaring this album. Probably the best summer of my life in terms of music? This is one of many 2001 records on this list.
_Let's get this out of the way: the Blue Album is arguably my favorite Weezer record, but Green is the one that got me into Weezer, and prompted the deep dive back into their earlier albums._

I had a [Green Album poster](photo:assets/40/photos/weezer-green-poster-flat.jpg) on my childhood bedroom wall. It's one of the only posters I can remember from that room, before I moved into the basement. I can remember studying it up close, dissecting every sticker on Rivers' guitar, and I _still_ want a lightning bolt guitar strap. That summer I got my first pair of Converse All Stars, navy blue low tops. Because that was what people who listened to Weezer wore, right??

I'd crank this album night and day on my Frankensteined speaker system: I cut a bunch of holes in a sheet of plywood, took apart every speaker in the house, and reassembled them in a massive wall built into my bookshelf. I was still early in learning how to play the bass, and I loved that I could play along to all these songs.
This album takes me right back to my childhood bedroom. Blue carpet, red bed frame, green album.
albums.label: Geffen Records

albums.title: What It Is to Burn
blurb: _What It Is to Burn_ isn't a record that just shaped me. I made it my **entire identity**, from the second semester of freshman year until _Deja Entendu_ came out at the end of sophomore year.

That Drive-Thru Records era got me good. The bands, the personalities, the behind-the-scenes DVDs that I watched about a thousand times. It was almost like that label was built in a lab just for me. The pop punk I loved in 2001 evolved into pure post-hardcore, and Finch was my favorite band to come out of that whole era. "Post Script" is still my favorite song on the album. I practiced those harmonics for hours to get them just right.

I was in a hilarious band with my buddies from high school. We changed our name half a dozen times, practiced relatively constantly but only played a handful of shows. Mostly we played Finch covers in Rob's basement and got yelled at to turn it down every ten minutes. Shoutout to my Waffle House Punk/Flatline/My City Arson fam.

I first saw Finch in February 2003 at Mississippi Nights with The Used, My Chemical Romance, and The Movielife. That lineup is insane, and it's still one of my favorite shows of all time. That June they played [Pointfest](photo:assets/40/photos/pointfest-15-ticket-2003.jpg "Pointfest 15, June 8, 2003") on a tiny stage by the entrance to Riverport, and their crowd was massive. We were front row, and the crowd stretched back as far as I could see.

After the show, my bandmates and I somehow ended up at their tour bus (no idea how) and met R2K, Nate, and the bassist, Derek. I asked Derek how he got his hair so crazy and wild — he had kind of a Robert Smith thing going — and he told me to just never wash it. I took that advice. A little too far. I didn't wash my hair for like a month. It was disgusting, and it looked nothing like his. I should have known better than to take grooming advice from a guy who lived on a tour bus.

Real Finch heads will remember there was never just one version of these songs. Between the _Falling Into Place_ EP, the Drive-Thru comps and the original demo of "What It Is to Burn," there were different versions of almost every song floating around. My burned CD mixes pulled from all of those releases, so I was mixing versions indefinitely. FWIW I still like the original "What It Is to Burn" way better.

One of the most prized records in my collection is the 2013 Hot Topic reissue on teal marble vinyl, only 1,500 pressed. The cover art is _extremely_ pixelated, and the name of the album on the labels is _What Is It to Burn_. Classic. Someone needs to pay the Hot Topic designers more.

albums.title: Glow On
blurb: This is an album that cracked open an entirely new genre for me. I don't know if Turnstile set out to make an "approachable" hardcore album, but it paved the way for me to explore it. I'd shied away from hardcore because it was always somewhat intimidating to me, but something about the time, place, and _pace_ of this album clicked, and I went looking for more.

I'm not sure if "Mystery" was served to me by the Spotify algorithm, shared by a friend, or popped up in my Instagram feed, but it was earth-shattering when it found me. The energy, the guitars, the melody, the VOLUME. Apparently it was something I was in desperate need of, because I ate that shit up. We had people over to our new house, and by the end of the night my brother and I were in control of the sound system, [headbanging in our unfinished kitchen](photo:assets/40/photos/turnstile-kitchen-2021.jpg "Unfinished kitchen mosh, June 2021
Photo by [@otisweekly](https://www.instagram.com/otisweekly/)"), blaring it as loud as it would go.

_Glow On_ came out a couple months later and immediately overtook everything on my radar. Usually when I fall in love with a single, the full album doesn't hit the same. This one delivered. And it blew up for a lot more people than just me. Turnstile became an incredibly popular band, and it felt like they could do no wrong. They were super creative, made artistic music videos, and broke the mold of what a hardcore album is supposed to be.

I saw Turnstile in April '22 on the _Glow On_ tour, and it was one of the most fun and chaotic concerts I've ever been to. I had never seen that much crowd surfing and stage diving in my life. People were taking Doc Martens to the face and leaving the pit bloody. They also played some older stuff from _Time & Space_, which got me to revisit the album I'd shelved shortly after it came out in 2018. It quickly started fighting _Glow On_ for airtime in my headphones.

This album jump-started a special phase in my life: a new house, a baby on the way, and a need for higher-energy tunes. It's my 6th most scrobbled album on Last.fm since I started tracking my plays in 2013, and I'm not sick of it yet.

albums.title: Country Grammar
albums.discovered: 2000, a sampler CD from my cousin
blurb: If you're from St. Louis, you know every word to this album. You don't need to know why this is on my list. For everyone else... ahem... rap wasn't "from" St. Louis. My favorite rappers were West Coast, East Coast, or Atlanta. Then Nelly showed up and suddenly St. Louis was cool?? In 2000 he was basically our Beatles. You couldn't go anywhere without hearing him.

This album happened _to me_. I didn't happen to find it. The whole city was losing its mind over the Super Bowl win and the incredible run the Cardinals were on. Nelly was the soundtrack to all of it, and owning this album was obligatory.

My cousin somehow got his hands on [an early promo sampler](photo:assets/40/photos/nelly-sampler-cd.jpg "Country Grammar promo sampler, Universal, 1999") with a few songs on it, but only a snippet of each. I remember riding around listening to it in his teal green Mitsubishi 3000GT. Eventually he gave it to me, and I must have played that "Ride wit Me" clip 10,000 times.

When the album finally dropped that summer, everyone I knew had it memorized. The St. Lunatics fashion was iconic: the Band-Aid under the eye, the backwards jerseys, the headbands, the Air Force 1s... I mean I couldn't pull any of that off but I wish I could have.
Twenty-six years later, I still can't get through a St. Louis wedding without "Ride wit Me," "E.I.," and "Country Grammar." And I still know every word.

> So feel me when I bring it,
> sing it loud (What?)

> I'm from the Lou' and
> I'm proud

albums.title: The Satanic Satanist
blurb: I can't remember the exact first time I heard Portugal. The Man, but I can pretty much guarantee it was late at night in the computer lab while listening to one of my Pandora stations. The instrumentation, the hooks, and the melodies of the songs on this album grabbed me right away. Then they turned around and put out _American Ghetto_ the next year, and _In the Mountain in the Cloud_ the year after that. Three albums in three years. They were on a hot streak.

That fall was my last semester at Mizzou, and I was making gig posters for pretty much anyone who'd let me. My buddy Paule and I did one for their show at Mojo's in Columbia: [Sisyphus pushing his boulder up a mountain](photo:assets/40/photos/ptm-sisyphus-poster-2010.jpg "Our poster for Forrest Rose Park, October 6, 2010"), inspired by "1000 Years." [Tickets were twelve bucks](photo:assets/40/photos/ptm-mojos-ticket-2010.jpg "Forrest Rose Park at Mojo's, October 6, 2010"). I made a bunch of gig posters in college, but this was the first time a band reached out to compliment me on one. They even signed a copy for me, which the venue then kept. Thieves.
Every time I hear this album, I get the same feeling I had that last fall semester: wanting to get the hell out of CoMo.
albums.label: Equal Vision

albums.title: Lonesome Dreams
blurb: This album is made for long drives and wide open skies, and it's the one that reminds me the most of Colorado. 2013 was our first year living here, and it felt like we were in a different part of the state every weekend. This was playing on every drive: Megan, Henry, and me, smelling like campfire and feeling very thankful for this beautiful place.

We saw them in March [at the Bluebird](photo:assets/40/photos/lord-huron-bluebird-2013.jpg "The Bluebird Theater, March 27, 2013"), then we saw them at Snowmass Mammoth Fest in June and went to their after show somewhere up in Snowmass Village. We showed up about an hour before anyone else, and the band was still setting up, so naturally we did tequila shots with them. Then we were [front row the whole night](photo:assets/40/photos/lord-huron-snowmass-2013.jpg "The after show in Snowmass Village, June 8, 2013"). It was an incredible time. It's not very often you get to discover a band and then see them a few months later in a super intimate setting.
I played it on a drive to the airport recently to give it a fresh listen before posting it here. I made it to the third song before I had tears in my eyes. It's crazy how far away 13 years can feel.

albums.title: Nearer My God
blurb: Foxing are from St. Louis, but if they were from LA or NYC they would be 100 times more famous than they are. This album dominated my 2018, it was my favorite record that year.
It was impossible to be an emo kid from STL and not have "Rory" pop up in your group chats. _The Albatross_ and _Dealer_ are fantastic records, but this album… this album was different.

It came out towards the end of Megan and my year-long trip around the globe. I remember long bus rides and long flights with this album downloaded to my Spotify account. I was probably the only person in Myanmar to listen to that record that year. Or maybe ever? It brought me back to reality a bit.

My buddy Kyle was in a band with two of the guys when they were younger, which, by association, makes _me_ very cool. I've seen them more times than I can count between Chicago and Denver, including a UMS set where Conor was absolutely furious with the fact they were essentially playing a street festival. They just kept getting better and better, and tighter and tighter as a band on stage.

Before one show at Subterranean, Jim (of course) and I decided to hit up the brand-new ✨Taco Bell Cantina✨ on Milwaukee Ave. We got the boozy slushies and immediately regretted it. I've never been sicker at a show, but then our second winds kicked in and we went to Mac DeMarco at the Metro for the second half of a double feature.
albums.label: Triple Crown

albums.title: Bon Iver, Bon Iver
blurb: _For Emma, Forever Ago_ and the _Blood Bank_ EP were core listening for any self-loathing sad boi like myself. I loved _For Emma_, but the self-titled record felt bigger and more complete to me. It brought everything together into a falsetto masterpiece of feels. I started my first "real" big boy job about a week after it came out, and it was the soundtrack to my L rides for months. I'm not in love with anything he's done since, but the Volcano Choir records are a fantastic companion to the first two Bon Iver albums.

I took French in high school, so I know how to pronounce it correctly. I've gotten in fights over this. It's very important to me. It's also perfect winter music, and I got to see them at the UIC Pavilion in December 2011 with Megan and my roommate Kelsey. Kelsey had tears in her eyes, so I asked if she was okay. "No, of course not. I just saw Bon Iver."
albums.label: Jagjaguwar

albums.title: Home, Like Noplace Is There
blurb: In the summer of 2014 I was on a contract at Dropbox, working super late nights and living in corporate housing for about two months. I was having a blast at work, but it was hard being away from Megan and Henry. I kept hearing about this album from my emo brethren in our group chat, so one night I put it on in the office while I was working on an installation. I was hooked three and a half minutes into the first song, right at the "FUCK!!" Hard to ignore a hook like that.

This record opened a new chapter in my life. It was emo revival, and it brought emo back into my life again. I spent college, and the few years after in Chicago, exploring more genres and styles than I ever had before, but this album single-handedly reminded me of who I was.

Yes, another 2014 album. This one got me back into loud, energetic, and unapologetic music. After it, bands like PUP, Hop Along, The World Is a Beautiful Place & I Am No Longer Afraid to Die, Turnstile, Oso Oso, Dogleg, Fiddlehead, Glitterer, and Teen Mortgage started showing up on my albums of the year lists, which meant new emo bands on my lists for the first time in nearly a decade. Oso Oso even opened for The Hotelier when I saw them at Beat Kitchen in October 2015. Would I have gotten into them without The Hotelier? Maybe. But _Home, Like Noplace Is There_ set something off in me that only the loudest, most energetic music could satisfy.

Ironically, almost everyone would say _Goodness_ is The Hotelier's masterpiece, and I just couldn't get into it. The mix hurts my ears! I am sensitive! _Home_ is the only record of theirs that does anything for me.

albums.title: Getting Killed
blurb: I had another album in this spot, but the [Geese show at Mission Ballroom last night](photo:assets/40/photos/geese-mission-ballroom-2026.jpg "Mission Ballroom, October 28, 2026") was so fantastic that they steamrolled their way onto this list.

_Getting Killed_ came out last fall and almost immediately became my album of the year. I listened to it on repeat for like six straight months. It awoke something in me, it was all I wanted to listen to. It's refreshing to hear real rock 'n' roll like this today, let alone from a band in their early twenties. About six weeks after it came out, I texted my emo group chat that it was "probably in the top five of my top ten albums of the last ten years." By February I was learning the bass lines and calling it maybe one of my top ten albums of all time?? What spell did Cameron Winter cast on me???

This was the first I'd ever heard of Geese or Cameron Winter actually. Funny enough, I'm not really into his solo stuff, even though that's apparently what won over Kenny Beats, who produced this record. Anything Kenny touches is gold, and _Getting Killed_ pulled me in, so much so that soon their prior album _3D Country_ made its way into my unstoppable vortex of Geese.

I felt a little weird putting an album that's just over a year old on a list of records that shaped me. But this album is so good, from such a talented band, that I hope they keep riding this lightning for many years to come.

albums.title: Mean Everything to Nothing
blurb: This was the first I'd ever heard of Manchester Orchestra. The album has incredible riffs and powerful hooks, and it was another record I put on in the print lab at Mizzou to get me through those all-night sessions.

This album became my workout record. My pump-up record. My record with all the feels. I was 22, I'd just signed up for an extra year and a half of college, and most of my friends were graduating that May without me. I had no idea what this budding graphic design major would bring me, or if it was worth the extra time spent in CoMo. "Everything to Nothing" is my favorite track: that riff, the power of those guitars, and a verse that said pretty much verbatim what I was thinking.

> I don't know what to do
> Not anymore
> Not anymore
It got me through a lot of different moments during that time in my life.

The album also kept that fire going right when I was moving away from emo in college. For years, they were my bridge from the Brand New and Taking Back Sunday days to The Hotelier. This album kicked off a nearly decade-long love affair with this band, and I even converted Megan. They always seemed to be on tour, and I feel like I've seen them ten times, all over the place.

In 2015 a group of us went back to Columbia for homecoming, and Manchester Orchestra playing the Blue Note that night was a big part of the appeal for me. After a full day of tailgating, I dragged everyone to the show. We were all a mess. Their sound has changed a lot since, and _A Black Mile to the Surface_ was the last record of theirs I really liked. But from their 2006 debut through that one, that's five albums I love, which is a lot for any band. That run, and the respect I have for them, earned them this spot.

albums.title: (What's the Story) Morning Glory?
blurb: This album needs no introduction.

My dad wouldn't let us have the CD because the last song talked about getting high. So, like most good albums of my youth, I heard it at a friend's house. I remember a few of us singing "Champagne Supernova" in my friend's bathroom without a single clue what any of it meant. In my defense, [Noel doesn't know what it means either](photo:assets/40/photos/oasis-noel-no-clue-stereogum.jpg "Noel on SiriusXM, September 2020
Via [Stereogum](https://stereogum.com/2100547/oasis-champagne-supernova-noel-gallagher/news/)").

Oasis were arguably the biggest band on the planet, but beyond this one, I didn't really listen to their other albums until college. Junior or senior year of high school, I went back and listened to the whole thing instead of just the singles. "Hello" and "Morning Glory" were darker, moodier, and heavier than I remembered, and I'd never realized how amazing those songs were back in elementary school. (Because, duh.)

Then in college I got really into their live album, _Familiar to Millions_. "Fuckin' in the Bushes" became my ultimate pump-up song, and I put it on our lacrosse warm-up mix that we played before every game. That's when I really discovered "Supersonic" and "Acquiesce," which sent me back to _Definitely Maybe_ and _The Masterplan_, both of which came out when I was way too young for them. I got to experience basically their entire discography (the "good" records at least 😬) all in one big, chaotic chunk, right when I had the most time to listen to music: college.

I've been a staunch defender of Oasis ever since. They're hilarious. They're annoying. They're everything rock 'n' roll stars should be. So naturally, when they announced they were getting back together, it was my chance to finally see them.

If you hung out with me at all last year, Oasis was all I could talk about. I revisited every album, talked about them nonstop, and got way too into [Liam's Twitter](photo:assets/40/photos/oasis-liam-acqeuse-tweet-2019.jpg "November 12, 2019
Via [x.com/liamgallagher](https://x.com/liamgallagher/status/1194229250863316992)").

I saw them at [Soldier Field in Chicago](photo:assets/40/photos/oasis-soldier-field-2025.jpg "Soldier Field, August 28, 2025"), and it was easily a top five concert of my life. No, top three. The energy, the production, the sound. It was perfect.
albums.label: Creation Records

albums.title: Hail to the Thief
blurb: WHAT? _Hail to the Thief_? Yes, _Hail to the Thief_. Not _Kid A_, _OK Computer_, or _In Rainbows_. I love those albums too, but this one is my favorite Radiohead album. Maybe it's because it's another album that lived in the CD player in my Jeep. Maybe it's because it was dark and moody. Or maybe it's because it's just plain **incredible**.
The first time I heard anything from the album was the "There There" video. I already knew I liked Radiohead, but this sounded creepy, and it intrigued me.
I love the album art. It was one of the CDs in my massive CD binder that I actually bought instead of downloaded. A prestigious honor.

I wish the instrumental bridge in "We Suck Young Blood" was a hundred minutes long. It's my favorite part of the album, and it's so short. In 2012 I [tweeted](https://x.com/R_O_P_E_R/status/212683240694218752) that it "might be my favorite 20 seconds of any Radiohead song ever."

I saw them on the _In Rainbows_ tour with, guess who, Jim, at the Verizon Wireless Amphitheater on May 14, 2008. We showed up without tickets, somehow scored unused friends and family tickets, and [ended up with seats](photo:assets/40/photos/radiohead-ticket-2008.jpg "Verizon Wireless Amphitheater, May 14, 2008"). It's one of the best light and stage shows I've ever seen. I've seen them since at Coachella in 2012 and Lollapalooza in 2016. Incredible live band.

albums.title: Merriweather Post Pavilion
blurb: Is there anything more fitting than Animal Collective and art school?

A few days into January 2009, my buddy Jim texted me that he'd found a leak and it was probably the album of the year. I'll never forget that text. I don't remember the exact first time I heard _Merriweather Post Pavilion_, but I listened to it the most in the screen-printing studio in the Mizzou art building that spring, and that's still where this album takes me.
It became the soundtrack to the spring semester of my senior year, and it dominated my entire 2009.

It feels like the right record to start this countdown with. It was one of my favorites almost from the first listen, barely a week into the year. And it came out right about halfway through my life so far. Right in the middle felt like the best place to start.

albums.title: Deja Entendu
blurb: Tonight I'm seeing Brand New at the Aragon in Chicago on the _Devil and God_ 20th anniversary tour. Yes, I realize this post isn't about _Devil and God_. It's about the album that started my unhealthy obsession with this band.

Nothing hit me harder at the time than _Deja Entendu_. It came out in 2003, still in the honeymoon period with my car, when I'd go out of my way to cruise around just to listen to music. I already knew every word to _Your Favorite Weapon_, but "Jude Law and a Semester Abroad" had nothing on the energy and intensity of this record. It felt grown up.

This was peak early-2000s me: skate and snowboard culture, emo, and plenty of teen angst. Winamp was always open, and I downloaded every _Deja_ demo and live song I could find on Kazaa. (LimeWire? BearShare? I'm dating myself.)

I remember catching the video for "The Quiet Things That No One Ever Knows" on what must have been MTV2. Vinnie's stupid hat. The car crash. Even the blue-green hue of the color grade has stuck with me.
It was the only thing in my CD player at Hidden Valley, and if you've been to that ditch outside St. Louis, you know most of your time is spent on the lifts. This album got a lot of chairlift time.

The original 2003 vinyl was 1,000 copies and near impossible to find. Twelve years later, it finally got repressed as a Record Store Day exclusive, limited to 1,400 copies. My buddy Jim and I got in line at 10 p.m. the night before with a cooler of beer. We ordered pizza, met fellow record enthusiasts, and stayed up all night being stupid. We had no idea how many copies they'd have, but we were [first in line](photo:assets/40/photos/deja-rsd-2015-lime.jpg "Record Store Day, April 18, 2015"), so we knew we'd get at least one. This is one of the only albums I'd ever do that for.
That night took the obsession to diabolical levels, much to Megan's disgust. My "emo" buddies are always happy to fuel it. Misery loves company.

Nowadays this one's more about nostalgia than actually listening to it. _The Devil and God Are Raging Inside Me_ is the one I'd rather put on. But _Deja_ stopped me in my tracks at 16, so it had to be the one on this list.

albums.title: Is the Is Are
blurb: I was never really into My Bloody Valentine or Slowdive or any of the bigger names in shoegaze, but _Is the Is Are_ was melodic and beautiful, and started me down a fuzzy, buzzy path with the genre.

I'd seen their first album, _Oshin_, on Pitchfork and a few other blogs when it came out. I liked it, but I never fully DIIVed into it (😭 _pun intended_). This one convinced me to give _Oshin_ another shot, and this time it clicked. I've loved everything they've released since, and they're one of my current favorite bands. They also cracked the door open for a lot more fuzz on my albums-of-the-year lists since.

The album is 17 tracks and over an hour long, and I didn't care one bit. I bought the limited-edition 2xLP and had it playing constantly. It's my 7th most scrobbled album on Last.fm, and it would rank even higher if all those vinyl plays counted.

One night I dropped the first record on the floor while the second one was playing (I _may_ have been intoxicated… doubtful, though). It slid all over the hardwood floor and got completely wrecked. When I woke up the next day, I found it, still on the floor, realized it was unplayable, and promptly reordered the exact same limited-edition 2xLP set. Now I own one copy of the first disc and two copies of the second. If anyone needs a spare second disc of _Is the Is Are_, let me know.

This album came out a few months before our wedding, so all of our planning happened to the soundtrack of _Is the Is Are_. I still remember recording a video for Meg on Valentine's Day with "Under the Sun" blaring in the background. She says this record is "perfect fall music," but I think it fits any time of year. It's one of a handful of records that can transport me to a specific moment in time: cold mornings taking [Henry](photo:assets/40/photos/henry-chicago-loft.jpg "Henry in the loft") on long walks to Lake Michigan, and our loft in Chicago, probably our favorite place we've ever lived.

blurb: I found _An Awesome Wave_ on Rdio in September 2012, which was about a day too late to see them at the Empty Bottle. The album cover intrigued me, "Breezeblocks" convinced me, and "Something Good" hooked me. It was weird and wonderful from the first ten seconds of the intro track, and I think only The xx has a better debut intro... but it's close.

By December I was telling friends it was my album of the year. When Rdio shut down in 2015, the [goodbye page](photo:assets/40/photos/rdio-farewell-2015.jpg "Rdio's goodbye page, December 2015") said I'd logged 1,853 hours on the app, with _An Awesome Wave_ as my most played album and "Something Good" as my most played song.

This is the album that reminds me most of our first apartment in Denver, living with my brother and our insane one-year-old border collie. I got the album on vinyl at their show at the Bluebird a couple of months after we moved here, and it's one of the first records I ever owned.

albums.title: Classics
blurb: _Classics_ came out right at the start of my sophomore year at Mizzou, and it's pretty much the sound of that fall for me. Headphones loud as hell, walking between classes, crunching through leaves, dodging the crazies at Speaker's Circle.

I was listening on the new iPod with video, which I student-charged at the Mizzou bookstore (it felt like free money at the time). It was my first iPod with a color screen, so naturally I spent hours making sure every album in my library had its cover art.

This album looked especially good on that screen, because the cover is black and gold. MIZ. There's a ferocious cat on the front. Not a tiger, but who cares. Close enough. And the iTunes bonus track it came with is called "Truman," so I'm counting it as a good omen.
_Classics_ sent me back to their first album, _Ratatat_, and it was just as good. I played those two so much they eventually blended into one long album in my head.

Those two albums, plus their third album, _LP3_, were basically my soundtrack to the design program. Late nights in the computer lab, empty energy drink cans, Domino's, the smell of printer ink, the hum of the iMacs. I also worked at the Student Design Center, which is where I got obsessed with gig posters and never really recovered. My boss there, Garrett, made a [poster](photo:assets/40/photos/ratatat-blue-note-2009-grain.jpg "Ratatat at The Blue Note, March 24, 2009
Poster by [@garrettkarol](https://www.instagram.com/garrettkarol/)") for their March 2009 show at The Blue Note that's still one of my favorite gig posters ever.

It's been over ten years since _Magnifique_. Evan put out an E.VAX record this year and Mike started a new band, which is great, but I think we all know what needs to happen here. WE'RE ALL WAITING FOR A NEW ALBUM, GUYS.

albums.title: Morning View
albums.discovered: Pretty sure my brother and I got this CD on release day.
blurb: Incubus is easily on my Mount Rushmore of bands. Picking one album is impossible. But these are the rules, even if I made them myself.

_S.C.I.E.N.C.E._, _Make Yourself_, _Morning View_ and _A Crow Left of the Murder_ are the Mount Rushmore of Incubus albums. This is not debatable. (_Light Grenades_ is fine.) _Make Yourself_ got me into Incubus, and _S.C.I.E.N.C.E._ got me digging deeper into the funkadelic sound they were capable of, but _Morning View_ cemented them on my all-time favorites list.

Incubus was already everywhere around 2000 because of "Drive," "Pardon Me" and Brandon Boyd's tremendous six-pack. _Morning View_ was a very highly anticipated follow-up to _Make Yourself_ from seemingly the entire world, and I was obsessed with the idea of the band living together in a house to record it. The [MTV Cribs episode](photo:assets/40/photos/incubus-cribs-house.jpg "The Morning View house on MTV Cribs, March 2001
Via [r/incubus](https://www.reddit.com/r/incubus/comments/1d3onp9/mtv_cribs_incubus_morning_view_house/)") was the literal dream for me, an [inside look](photo:assets/40/photos/incubus-cribs-brandon.jpg "Brandon Boyd answering the door
Via [r/incubus](https://www.reddit.com/r/incubus/comments/1d3onp9/mtv_cribs_incubus_morning_view_house/)") at the album being made. I would have killed to hang out in that house.

Dirk Lance was one of my favorite bass players, and I was still learning the bass in 2001. The bass lines on this album changed my life (not hyperbole). I practiced these songs until my fingers hurt. "Are You In?" and "Have You Ever" were, and still are, some of my favorites to play. I figured if I could play Incubus bass lines, I must be progressing. Turns out this is when I peaked. But I was hooked.

I had a gigantic album release poster on my wall. I must have gotten it off eBay, but it was huge, and I loved everything about it: the tilted angle of the photo, the bright orange type. I was into graphic design before I even knew what graphic design was.

When they announced their St. Louis stop, I bought tickets in person at Streetside Records the day they went on sale. I waited for the store to open and was first in line (okay I was the only one in line). I couldn't miss them. On September 12, 2002, they played UMB Bank Pavilion. It was the first time I had seats there instead of the lawn, and I picked stage left on purpose so I could be on Dirk's side. I was close enough to see the sweat on his face. I [laminated the ticket stub](photo:assets/40/photos/incubus-ticket-2002.jpg "UMB Bank Pavilion, September 12, 2002") so I could keep it forever.
Meg and I saw them play _Morning View_ in full at Ball Arena in 2024, and trust me, Brandon still has the abs.

albums.title: Third Eye Blind
albums.discovered: Summer 1997, on the radio. Really "heard" it a decade later.
blurb: If you were around in the summer of 1997, this album is permanently burned into your brain. It was everywhere. On the radio, on MTV, in movies. There was no escaping it. I was 10, and like everyone else, I knew every single word to "Semi-Charmed Life" and "How's It Going to Be." And I loved those songs. They were fun, they were loud, and they were slightly edgy for a soon-to-be 5th grader? (I obviously didn't know "Semi-Charmed Life" was about crystal meth...)

And that's kind of where my story with the album ended. Until college, when my roommate Ted went on and on about how amazing the entire tracklist was and how pivotal it was to our youth. When Third Eye Blind came to the Blue Note in Columbia two days after my 23rd birthday, he convinced us all to [get tickets](photo:assets/40/photos/teb-ticket-2009-stub.jpg "Remember paper tickets?"). Was it a school night? Yes. But as a super senior, it was my obligation to go. So I loaded the album onto my 160GB iPod Classic and realized I'd never really listened past the singles.

This album has absolutely no skips. The very first track, "Losing a Whole Year," is incredible, and _might_ be one of my favorite songs of all time. I became obsessed all over again, with the songs and with the feeling of summer '97. It's an album I'll play for a week straight, pretty much once a year, every year.

albums.title: From Under the Cork Tree
blurb: _From Under the Cork Tree_ was THE summer album for me the summer before my freshman year of college. It's probably the only album that can immediately take me back to those few months before I went away to Mizzou.

Everyone heard "Sugar, We're Goin Down" that spring, but the album didn't really hit me until we went to Destin, FL (like every St. Louisan) the first week of August. I played it on the beach, I played it for all the girls we met on the beach, I played it going to sleep, then played it on repeat the whole drive back to St. Louis.

It came with me to Mizzou that fall. One night I asked my dorm mate Chris, "What is a loaded god complex?" and without missing a beat he said, "I don't know, but it's got a cocker and puller!" That silly little quote is cemented in my brain for eternity. It's wit like that that got him the job as our wedding officiant 11 years later.

That November, Chris and I drove from Columbia to see them at the Pageant on the [Nintendo Fusion Tour](photo:assets/40/photos/fob-pageant-ticket-2005.jpg "Nintendo Fusion Tour, November 13, 2005") with The Starting Line, Motion City Soundtrack, Boys Night Out, and Panic! at the Disco. I mean, wow. That lineup was absolutely perfect for that moment in time. And finally, after maybe a hundred shows in my youth, I caught a [drumstick](photo:assets/40/photos/fob-hurley-stick.jpg "Andy Hurley's stick, 21 years later"). I'm pretty sure the drummer was tossing it to someone else, [but I pounced](photo:assets/40/photos/fob-pageant-drumstick-2005.jpg "The Pageant, November 13, 2005").
I can't believe this album is over 20 years old.
WAIT... I CAN'T BELIEVE I STARTED COLLEGE OVER 20 YEARS AGO.

blurb: I spent the fall of 2013 training for a marathon that never ended up happening, so the fall of 2014 was round two: endless training runs along the Chicago lakefront. _Run the Jewels 2_ came out right in the middle of it, and it's probably the only reason I finished my training (and the marathon). It's my second most-played album on Last.fm, and I'd bet half of those plays happened on the lakefront path. [These graphs](photo:assets/40/photos/rtj2-lastfm-scrobbles.png "My Last.fm scrobbles, 2014 and all time") don't lie.

The funny part is I'd been listening to Killer Mike since I was 14 without knowing it. He's featured on "Snappin' & Trappin'" on _Stankonia_, and I never thought twice about who he was. Fourteen years later, he was in my ears on every single long run. The features on this album are even more wild: Zack de la Rocha from Rage and the drum god himself Travis Barker.

RTJ felt like they were everywhere that fall and for years after. They played Lollapalooza in 2014, a few months before this came out, and I had no idea who they were. By the time I saw them there in 2017, I (and the rest of the world) definitely did.

albums.title: The Devil and God Are Raging Inside Me
blurb: _Deja Entendu_ got me into Brand New, and it shaped a lot of my early-2000s music taste. That was the band I thought I knew.

So when _The Devil and God Are Raging Inside Me_ came out in November 2006, my sophomore year at Mizzou, I wasn't ready for it. I didn't give it the time of day. I was ready to leave my emo-ness behind. (Same fall as Ratatat's _Classics_, if you're keeping track.)
It took developing an unhealthy obsession with _Daisy_ to actually go back. Most people hate _Daisy_. I loved the energy. And somewhere in my late 20s, _Devil and God_ finally clicked.
I haven't wanted to listen to _Deja_ in years. I'll never get sick of _Devil and God_.

I saw them play it front to back on the 10-year anniversary run in Milwaukee in 2016. Today I'm seeing the 20th anniversary tour at the Aragon in Chicago. Seeing this album every ten years is becoming a thing.

albums.title: Champ
blurb: _Champ_ is one of those albums where I couldn't name a single other song or album by the band. But this one hooked me from the moment I heard it.

It came out the summer before my last semester of college. I was in the home stretch of my design program, I knew I'd be a graphic designer, and I had my sights set on Chicago. I couldn't wait to get there.

This album takes me right back to my first apartment there, and the winter of my internship. I was on my own, truly for the first time, in a city I wasn't raised in and had barely visited, but I knew I wanted to be there. Cold walks down Division to my internship. Picante burritos. [PBR](photo:assets/40/photos/champ-pbr-bike.jpg "The water bottle holder. Used as intended. Chicago 2011"). I was learning how to really be an adult in a city that became my adopted home and still holds a special place in my heart.

That summer I met a girl at Lollapalooza. We flirted the only logical way you could in 2010: on Twitter. "Bambi" was one of the first songs I ever sent her, in a tweet on December 13, 2010. She ended up becoming my wife. I guess this album hooked her too.

From the first few notes of "Favourite Food," it punches me in the gut and puts a knot in my chest. It's one of the few albums that gives me a positive, visceral reaction every time, because it marks such a clear, and special, place in my life.

albums.title: Feed the Animals
blurb: To the surprise of absolutely no one who went to college with me, _Feed the Animals_ made the list.
If you passed me the aux at a party, in the car, or at the after-bars, I was putting this album on.
This kicked off an obsession with mashups that fueled almost a decade of my life. Super Mash Bros, The White Panda, The Hood Internet. I couldn't get enough.

Part of the appeal of Gregg Gillis was his live show. Stripping down to his underwear, hunched over a laptop covered in plastic wrap. Sweat everywhere. I saw him at IU a few months after _Feed the Animals_ came out. He let as many people on stage as would fit, and it was just a [giant dance party from start to finish](photo:assets/40/photos/girl-talk-jakes-2009.jpg "Girl Talk at Jake's, Bloomington, January 16, 2009").
I finally got it on vinyl a couple years ago. What a weird record to own on a physical medium.

albums.title: Plans
blurb: _Plans_ came out right as my freshman year of college started. [I bought it on iTunes](photo:assets/40/photos/plans-ipod.jpg "My coveted 3rd gen iPod") with gift cards I got for graduation. New friends, new experiences, a new home. I avoided the freshman fifteen, but the freshman blues hit me hard. I was only two hours from St. Louis, but I was homesick, even if I was pretending I wasn't. Fall always got me down, and this album couldn't have fit my mood better.
It's a record about change, distance and losing people, and how plans rarely go to plan. Pretty fitting for an 18-year-old who had no idea what the hell he was doing.

Fall semester was Hudson Hall, pizza from Rollins, football games ([rushing the field after we beat Nebraska](photo:assets/40/photos/plans-nebraska-2005.jpg "Faurot Field, October 22, 2005")), driving my dad's blue Camaro when my Jeep was in the shop. Feeling lost and always awkward.

This is another example of an album on this list that might not be considered a band's "best album," but it's probably my favorite. I loved _Transatlanticism_, but something about _Plans_, fall in mid-Missouri and living on a beautiful campus (and also living on Facebook) hit me hard because of where I was in life.

The tempo shift in the middle of "Different Names for the Same Thing" is my favorite part of the album. The first time I heard it, I thought, "Ugh, this is just a sad piano song, and I'm not really into those." I almost skipped to the next track. Then, right around the two-minute mark, it completely overtook me. "Crooked Teeth" is another favorite, and for a moment made me feel like everything was going to be alright. Until I learned the song was about a dead-end relationship. That Ben Gibbard. What a treasure.
This album still gives me a little heartache every time I hear it because of where it takes me.

blurb: I'd heard "Yellow" just about everywhere music was played when it came out, and enjoyed the song, but a year after the album was released a friend told me I needed to listen to the full album. We were in 9th grade English class. Why does my brain remember this stuff? The record was way more than just that single song, and I loved it from the moment I heard it. I fell back in love with the album a few years later when "Don't Panic" showed up in _Garden State_ and rediscovered _Parachutes_ after I had shelved it for _A Rush of Blood to the Head_.
This album kicked off a run of three albums I adore, even after _The 40-Year-Old Virgin_ made hating Coldplay cool. (To be clear I do not associate with anything after _X&Y_.)

Then this album took on a whole new meaning about 20 years later when Megan put it on her birthing playlist to welcome Wilson. He wasn't born to "Sparks," but it was on the playlist, and it's the one song that reminds me most of her pregnancy.

Two years later, we played this album while [Wilson colored all over the walls](photo:assets/40/photos/parachutes-wilson-walls.jpg "February 23, 2025") we were about to tear down for our renovation. It's one of the happiest, most peaceful moments in our house that I can remember.

blurb: I remember NPR putting up the full album stream a week before it came out, and I had it on repeat. I'm pretty sure I went to the record store the day it came out to buy it on vinyl.

And the cherry on top was [Draplin's](https://www.draplin.com/work/festivals/sasquatch) festival identity. The Gorge that spring was like the Super Bowl for graphic designers.

This album takes me back to our first apartment in Denver, my first year really getting into collecting vinyl (it was one of the first records I owned), exploring the mountains of Colorado, and being 26 years old and blissfully unaware of any real concerns in life.

albums.title: A Live One
blurb: And now for something completely different. This is the band I get the most shit for from my friends, and nearly 30 years later I'm still not budging. Blame it on going to a private middle school where everyone seemed to have an older brother into The Samples, Phish, DMB, and The String Cheese Incident. I never stood a chance.

Even our neighbor followed Phish around the country and had a Phish sticker on his 1990 Civic. I stared at that thing for years with no idea what it meant. Pretty soon there was [a Phish poster](photo:assets/40/photos/phish-poster.jpg) in my basement bedroom, one of three band posters in a sea of snowboarding posters and stickers.

This album takes me right back to mowing the grass for my allowance with my Sony Walkman and those behind-the-ear headphones. It's a two-disc set, and disc one got way more time in my CD player. In my defense, disc two has a 31-minute "Tweezer" on it. That's a big ask for a 7th grader.

I memorized all 21 minutes of "You Enjoy Myself." When I got my license, I'd drive my friends around in my Jeep playing whatever emo or rap they wanted. Then I'd drop off the last one and crank YEM for the ride home. Nobody had to know. (I never did save up for a five-disc changer, so disc one got spun until it skipped.)
_For the record: we did not name our firstborn after "Wilson." But it's a nice homage to an absolute banger. It's the first track on disc two, the one that got less play. Sorry, buddy._

Phish is probably the only band on this list I've never seen live, which is extra ironic for a live album. I'll fix that one day, and I'll be the 40-year-old first-timer slapping air bass through every minute of YEM.

albums.title: Stankonia
blurb: Quite possibly my favorite album of all time. _Stankonia_ came out a day before I turned 14 — thank you Big Boi and André 3000 for an amazing birthday present! I rode my bike to Streetside Records after school to buy the CD, then locked myself in the basement until I'd learned every single lyric. That night I remember hyping the album up on AOL Instant Messenger with my friends from school. Y2K ruled.
I was hooked from the intro:

> O-U-T-K-A-S-T
> Live, from the center of the Earth
> Seven light-years below sea level we go
> Welcome to Stankonia, the place from which all funky things come
> Would you like to come?
Then "Gasoline Dreams" kicked in, and those guitars punched me right in the mouth.

At the time I was obsessed with two things: football and music. (Okay, girls were third. Maybe second. Arguably first. But that's a story for another album blurb.) OutKast ended all their skits on this album with "BREAK!" There is love #1, football! And it seemed that everything else about this album (besides the drug use, inner city living, teen pregnancy, and street hustling) was like it was made for me. I didn't know why there were bombs over Baghdad, and I had no idea Spaghetti Junction wasn't a food dish. Just a 14-year-old from the St. Louis suburbs with a curfew and a bike. Totally relatable.

I will never get sick of this album. The beats, the album cover, and the melodies are etched into my memory. Obviously "Ms. Jackson," "B.O.B.," and "So Fresh, So Clean" were everywhere at the time, but I loved some of the deeper cuts even more, like "Humble Mumble," and the incredibly misunderstood (in my 14-year-old mind) "I'll Call B4 I Cum." My CD always skipped at the part in André 3000's verse in "Ms. Jackson": "Together dream 'bout that crib with the Goodyear-_year_ swing" and I thought the lyrics were "year-year swing" for like 15 years.

They say the music you love at 14 sticks with you for the rest of your life, and I started off STRONG. Love #2, music! Ten years ago, I [tweeted](photo:assets/40/photos/outkast-tweet-2016.jpg): "I don't do this website very often but I am so excited to show my future kids Outkast." Now I have kids, I've shown them _Stankonia_, and they couldn't care less. But one day they will.

albums.title: In Our Nature
blurb: José González is perfect fall music. Every time I hear _In Our Nature_, I think of fall. Which is funny, because my strongest memories of it are from spring.

It came out in September 2007, the fall of my junior year at Mizzou. I'd liked _Veneer_ a lot, but this one had some incredible melodies. And I loved the raw production: the backing metronome and foot taps on some of the songs, the creak of a chair, the scratch of the strings. Mostly just a guy and his guitar. That's not usually something that keeps me entertained for a whole album.

That spring, I listened to it on [every bus ride to our lacrosse away games](photo:assets/40/photos/jose-gonzalez-bus.jpg "On a bus somewhere"). Super long hours with all the guys, sleeping on the floor in the back, waking up every once in a while in the parking lot of a McDonald's or some other stop. We were more worried about partying that season than winning games, but we beat Kansas, which is all that mattered. My friends also shaved my head that spring. It's crazy the memories this album is tied to.
I can put it on any time and go right back to fall. And that bus floor.

albums.title: Miss Universe
blurb: _Miss Universe_ is my "Covid" album. It came out in March 2019, but it will never not remind me of the 2020 shutdown.

In November 2019, I went to [Pitchfork Paris](photo:assets/40/photos/nilufer-pitchfork-paris-2019.jpg "Nilüfer Yanya at Pitchfork Paris, November 1, 2019"). Nilüfer was playing on my actual birthday, and that's what convinced me to go. I got to say hi and told her she was the reason I came. She looked confused and asked, "Why?"
Then Covid happened. Suddenly I had tons of time to listen to music, and this album never left my rotation. It's still one of my most-played albums ever.
There was life before Covid and life after Covid. This album sits right on that line as a sort of weird bridge between the two realities we all had to accept.

Looking back, it's actually pretty fitting for a Covid album. The whole album has these interludes about a made-up wellness company called _WWAY Health_, short for "We Worry About Your Health." A year after the album came out, we all were.

albums.title: Jungle
blurb: _Jungle_ was the sound of my fall 2014. I first heard it in early August that year and played the absolute hell out of it on Rdio (RIP, the best streaming service of all time). It hit me and gripped me like a wild animal from the …jungle… for about ten years. And it's still one of my favorite albums to this day.
It was dancy. It was fun. It felt retro and modern at the same time. It felt brand new to me.

As a designer, there's something really pleasing about a band that uses the same cover art template for every album. Five albums in, they've stuck with it, and I admire that. The gold foil on this one was a pleasant surprise when I got it.
It's also on XL, one of my favorite labels and home to a few artists that have made (or will make) this list.

I've seen them a few times now, and [there's like a million people on stage](photo:assets/40/photos/jungle-mission-ballroom-2021.jpg "Jungle at Mission Ballroom, Denver, October 19, 2021"), each running around playing a different instrument. Their shows are so fun.

blurb: One more, because this list wouldn't be complete without it.

I first heard "Strangers" in _The Darjeeling Limited_, and Megan and I picked it for our wedding song in 2016. It isn't a love song. Dave Davies has said it's about getting through the hard stuff together, and a connection between people that's deeper than words. To me there's something spiritual in it. "We are not two, we are one." stuck with both of us, and it felt perfect for our first dance. I even [printed it on our wedding invites](photo:assets/40/photos/kinks-wedding-invite.jpg).

After the wedding I bought a vintage vinyl pressing of the album and started listening to it a lot, and the whole record really grew on me. I can't hear The Kinks now without thinking of our wedding day.

albums.title: Give Up
blurb: I knew who Death Cab was, so I knew Ben Gibbard and co., but I had no idea The Postal Service was even happening, and I don't think anyone really saw it coming.

I've always loved the band name. They made the album by physically mailing tracks back and forth, so they called themselves The Postal Service (even though I later learned they actually sent everything FedEx or UPS. Frauds.).
The first time I heard _Give Up_ was in a snowboarding movie. "Such Great Heights" is Bobby Meeks' part in _Lame_, the 2003 Robot Food film, and I watched that movie a hundred times with my brothers.
It was perfect snowboarding music, and it was the first time I really liked "electronic" music. I was _fully_ in my emo phase at the time, but this album opened my eyes to a world of other genres.

_Give Up_ also gave me one of the best rejections of my life. A girl I liked told me she wasn't interested in me anymore by sending me "Nothing Better" over AIM. It still stings a little how good that burn was.
The album kept growing on me over the years. Meg and I saw them play it at Sasquatch for the 10th anniversary. The shitty old iPhone videos don't do it justice.

albums.title: The Dream Is Over
blurb:
I was walking Henry by the lake when Jim texted me about a band I'd never heard of. Their new album was streaming online a week before it came out, and [people were already raving about it](photo:assets/40/photos/pup-ian-cohen-tweet-2016.jpg "
Via [x.com/en_cohen](https://x.com/en_cohen/status/733277351790841856)"). PUP was easily the stupidest band name I'd ever heard. Then I learned it stands for Pathetic Use of Potential, and that they used to be called Topanga, as in _Boy Meets World_. Okay, fine. Topanga was a babe.

I remember exactly where I was standing the first time I hit play: [the lakefront path, just south of Belmont Harbor](photo:assets/40/photos/pup-first-listen-map.jpg "First listen, May 19, 2016"). Thank god I had my headphones with me. It quickly became my album of the year in 2016, and after a few listens I went back to their first record, fell in love with that one too, and have seen them live about ten times since.

The first time was July 2016. It was supposed to be at Wicker Park Fest, but weather pushed it to Beat Kitchen, and they didn't go on until around midnight. So I was chugging Red Bulls with, guess who, Jim. I might have had an accident in the mosh pit. (More on that later.) That night kicked off a streak of very _not_ normal PUP shows for me:

- August 2017, Lolla aftershow at the Empty Bottle: sweat through and ripped the shirt I came in, and got [the best shirt they had at the merch table](photo:assets/40/photos/pup-lolla-aftershow-2017.jpg "Empty Bottle, August 3, 2017") to leave in. At some point I turned to my buddy Paule and said, "I think this is my favorite band ever."
- May 2019, Metro: [day drinking at a Cardinals-Cubs game at Wrigley](photo:assets/40/photos/pup-wrigley-hot-dog-2019.jpg "Wrigley Field, May 4, 2019") with Jim. PUP that night, then straight to the airport for a 5 a.m. flight. I slept at the gate.
- June 2019, Gothic Theatre: my first time seeing them in Denver. [Stefan crowd surfed and wrecked the entire first row](photo:assets/40/photos/pup-gothic-2019-contact.jpg "Front row = collateral damage
Gothic Theatre, June 29, 2019"). I broke my phone screen and lost my hat. Budweiser was involved.
- March 2020, [Ogden Theatre](photo:assets/40/photos/pup-ogden-2020.jpg "Ogden Theatre, March 5, 2020"): pretty sure that's where I got Covid for the first time.
- March 2023, Mission Ballroom, the second day of my paternity leave: I fainted, got a concussion, and pissed my pants. Ask me about it next time you see me.

This band makes fun music to be stupid to, and I spent most of my 30s being stupid to it. Megan has since banned me from ever seeing them live again. I wonder why? She did, however, [dress up as me for Halloween](photo:assets/40/photos/pup-halloween-tweet-2017.jpg) as a tribute to that first show. PUP liked the tweet.

albums.title: You've Come a Long Way, Baby
blurb: Fatboy Slim is ADD music for a very ADD kid.

I had no idea he was from England, and I probably wouldn't have cared. I didn't know what a DJ or a producer was, or why he was called Fatboy Slim. I just knew it didn't sound like anything I'd ever heard. I'm pretty sure my dad bought this CD and I just stole it from him. Did my dad introduce me to Fatboy Slim??
It was the edited version, because Walmart wouldn't sell anything with a Parental Advisory sticker. So to me, the lyrics to "In Heaven" will always be:

> Fatboy Slim is _illinin_ heaven
> Fatboy Slim is _illinin_ heaven
> Fatboy Slim is _illinin_ heaven

Last year I bought the vinyl reissue from Walmart.com, and 26 years later they finally sold me the uncensored version. I was/am obsessed with the cover: the wall of records (his actual collection!), and the little white glove-looking doodle on the shelf under his name. What even is that? I still don't know, does anyone know?
In 7th grade we did a dance to "The Rockafeller Skank" for spirit week and won over the crowd with our moves. (Just kidding. We were terrible.) And the "Praise You" video was all over MTV.
There's been a song from this album on every running playlist I've ever made, and "Gangster Tripping" is a regular play of mine at the bowling alley on league nights.

albums.title: Is This It
blurb: I really don't remember where or when I discovered this album. I think my brother Dean had the CD (who knows how he got it), and I probably stole it shortly after he brought it home. But I remember having it, and I remember that iconic logo on the disc. I love that logo. I'm pretty sure they ripped it off from something, and the graphic designer in me should be angry about that, but it's perfection.

_Room on Fire_ also rips, and it might be my favorite of their first two albums, but nothing beats the feeling this record gave me back then. The glamorous rock 'n' roll life, leather jackets, ripping cigs, living in New York. My St. Louis suburban brain could never fathom that lifestyle.

I thought [_Meet Me in the Bathroom_](photo:assets/40/photos/strokes-mmitb-poster.jpg "Meet Me in the Bathroom, 2022
Via [TMDB](https://www.themoviedb.org/movie/913792-meet-me-in-the-bathroom)") was a slightly "meh" documentary, but all that home footage of The Strokes took me right back to Sony Handycams and early-2000s skate videos. It felt like a DIY band with a DIY sound, and the riffs were infectious. This album transports me back to that time. A simpler time.

I finally saw them at Red Rocks on August 14, 2023. Julian was drunk as hell and rambling away, just as I wanted him to be. But then the songs would kick in, and he'd snap back into the insane performer he is.
I've put this album on repeat about once a quarter, every year, since it came out. It has no skips, it's so raw, and fun, and I've never gotten sick of it. Neither will you.

albums.title: Here and Nowhere Else
blurb: I'm one of the only people I know who really loves the first Cloud Nothings record. It was fun and fast, and I listened to it a ton that first year I was in Chicago.

Then they changed their sound to something much harder and more intense. There was no avoiding it, and _Attack on Memory_ is a fantastic record. But _Here and Nowhere Else_ struck the balance I was looking for at the time: energy, intensity, and fun.
2014 was a big year of music for me. I'd gone freelance, moved back to Chicago, and felt free in one of the best cities on the planet. So it's no coincidence this is another 2014 album.

A month after it came out, Jim and I saw them at Lincoln Hall. [Consequence of Sound reviewed the show](photo:assets/40/photos/cloud-nothings-cos-review-2014.jpg "Consequence of Sound, May 4, 2014
Via [consequence.net](https://consequence.net/2014/05/live-review-cloud-nothings-at-chicagos-lincoln-hall-53/)"), and the reviewer called out two guys in Cardinals gear shoving and shouting along to every word. That was us.

I've seen them maybe a dozen times, and whenever they play songs from this album, they're the best songs of the show. "Pattern Walks" is the one I want to see live more than any other. The ending is a cacophony of noise, and I've never seen another drummer smack the shit out of the drums like their drummer. He's like a Muppet back there going ham on those things.

Meg and I also went to a Cloud Nothings and Japandroids show at the Vic in November 2017, the last concert we saw as Chicago residents before moving away. So this band really opened and closed my chapter in Chicago.
Five albums later, Cloud Nothings still hasn't missed.
